warmup.q: merchants has 10,000 rows. Statistics say 10% are in Amsterdam and 10% are in NL, and every Amsterdam merchant is in NL. How many rows does PostgreSQL estimate for city = 'Amsterdam' AND country = 'NL' before you give it any extra statistics?
options: 1,000: it sees that the two columns go together
It filters a small sample at planning time and counts
warmup.why: PostgreSQL keeps statistics per column and combines conditions by multiplying their selectivities, which assumes the columns are independent: 10,000 x 0.1 x 0.1 = 100. The real count is 1,000, and the third Try it shows both numbers. Seeing that columns go together takes extended statistics (CREATE STATISTICS). Filtering a sample at planning time is what some other systems do for base tables; PostgreSQL reads only the stored statistics.

sections.h: The planner picks the plan it expects to be cheapest
sections.html:
Every night a report asks the payments database how many chargebacks hit merchants in Amsterdam. Three tables hold the answer: merchants (10,000 rows), payments (1,000,000) and chargebacks (20,000).

SELECT count(*) FROM merchants m
JOIN payments p ON p.merchant_id = m.id
JOIN chargebacks c ON c.payment_id = p.id
WHERE m.city = 'Amsterdam';

SQL says what you want, never how to compute it. The executor from lesson 9, a tree of operators that pull rows from each other, needs a plan: which two tables to join first, which side of each join is the outer one, and which join method to use for each (nested loop, hash or merge, also from lesson 9). Count the plans for this query. There are two join orders (merchants with payments first, or payments with chargebacks first), two choices of outer side at each of the two joins, and three methods at each join: 2 x 4 x 9 = 72 plans, before you count indexes. All of them return the same number. Some take milliseconds and some take minutes.

Version 1 of a planner runs every plan and keeps the fastest. That costs more than running the worst plan once, so nobody does it.

Version 2 predicts what each plan will cost without running it. PostgreSQL's cost model counts work in made-up units in which reading one 8 KB page in sequence costs 1.0 (seq_page_cost). A random page read costs 4.0, handling one row costs 0.01 (cpu_tuple_cost), and evaluating one operator such as > costs 0.0025 (cpu_operator_cost). A sequential scan of payments reads 6,370 pages and 1,000,000 rows, so it costs 6,370 x 1.0 + 1,000,000 x 0.01 = 16,370. Add a WHERE clause and every row also pays for one comparison: 2,500 more. The Try it checks both numbers against EXPLAIN.

The formula has a hole. The page count of a table is known, because pg_class.relpages stores it. But the cost of the operator above the scan depends on how many rows come out of the scan, and the cost of a join depends on how many rows come out of both of its inputs. Nobody knows those numbers until the query runs, so the planner guesses them. The guess is the cardinality estimate: how many rows each step of a plan will produce.

So a cost-based optimizer has three parts, shown in the figure. One lists the possible plans, one estimates the rows at every step, and one turns rows and pages into a cost. The planner picks the plan with the lowest cost. The cost model is a few formulas you can check by hand. The estimates are where plans go wrong, and the rest of this lesson is about them.

try.title: Check the cost model by hand
steps: From labs/, start PostgreSQL with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait and open psql with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz. The first statement drops this lesson's tables if an earlier run left them.
Create merchants, payments (with an index on merchant_id) and chargebacks; every Try it in this lesson uses them. Then read relpages and reltuples for payments.

Predict the total cost of SELECT * FROM payments with the formula above, and how much the WHERE clause adds. Then run the two EXPLAINs. The cost is the second number in cost=0.00..16370.00; the first is the cost before the first row comes out.

sections.h: Row estimates come from a small summary of each column
sections.html:
Take WHERE amount_cents < 1000 on payments. The planner needs the fraction of rows that pass, called the selectivity, and it can't read a million rows to find it.

Version 1 knows only the smallest and largest amount, 0 and 99,997, and assumes the values spread evenly between them. Then 1,000 is 1% of the way along, so 1% of the rows pass: 10,000. The real count is 215,410, because most payments are small. The Try it's amounts pile up at the low end the way card payments do, many coffees and few laptops, and the even-spread guess is 20 times too low.

Version 2 keeps a small summary of each column's shape. ANALYZE, which autovacuum also runs for you, reads a random sample of 30,000 rows (300 times default_statistics_target, which defaults to 100) and stores for every column, in the pg_stats view:

  • null_frac, the fraction of nulls, and n_distinct, how many different values there are;
  • most_common_vals with most_common_freqs: up to 100 values that are clearly more common than the rest, each with its share of the rows;
  • histogram_bounds: 101 values that cut the other rows into 100 buckets with the same number of rows each.

That last one is an equi-depth histogram. Its buckets don't have equal widths, they have equal depths: each holds 1% of the rows. Where amounts are dense the buckets are narrow (in the Try it the first bounds are 51, 125 and 169 cents) and where they are sparse they are wide (the last bucket runs from 97,124 to 99,985). The figure shows the same idea with 10 buckets.

To estimate amount_cents < v, the planner counts the whole buckets below v, then assumes the values inside the one bucket that holds v spread evenly, and adds that fraction of a bucket. PostgreSQL's docs write it as (i + (v - lo) / (hi - lo)) / buckets, where lo and hi are the bounds of bucket i. The uniformity assumption is still there, but only inside one narrow bucket, so the error stays small. Common values are added from the MCV list separately. The Try it estimates 213,802 rows against 215,410 real ones.

Equality uses the MCV list. city = 'Amsterdam' is a common value with frequency 0.1, so the estimate is 10,000 x 0.1 = 1,000, exactly right. For a value not in the list, PostgreSQL assumes the rows the common values don't cover are shared evenly by all the other distinct values: (1 - sum of MCV frequencies) / (n_distinct - number of MCVs).

A join needs one more formula. For p.merchant_id = m.id, the basic estimate is rows(p) x rows(m) / max(distinct merchant_id, distinct m.id): 1,000,000 x 10,000 / 10,000 = 1,000,000, one row per payment. That is right for a foreign key, and it assumes every merchant id in payments finds its merchant.

sections.h: Correlated columns break the independence assumption
sections.html:
A reporting screen has three dropdowns, city, country and currency, and the ORM puts all three into the WHERE clause: city = 'Amsterdam' AND country = 'NL' AND currency = 'EUR'. The statistics say each condition keeps 10% of the merchants. What does the AND keep?

PostgreSQL multiplies: 0.1 x 0.1 x 0.1 = 0.001, so 10 merchants out of 10,000. That is the independence assumption: knowing that a merchant is in Amsterdam tells you nothing about its country. For unrelated columns, such as the currency of a payment and the hour it was made, it is close enough. Here it is absurd. Every Amsterdam merchant is in NL and takes EUR, so the AND keeps the same 1,000 merchants that the city alone keeps. In the Try it, one condition is estimated at 1,000 rows, two at 100 and three at 10, while the real count stays at 1,000. Each extra correlated condition divides the estimate by 10.

An error at the bottom of a plan doesn't stay there. The join above uses the 10 as its input, so it expects 10 x 100 = 1,000 payments and gets 100,000, and the next join multiplies again. In a 2015 study, Leis and colleagues measured this with the Join Order Benchmark, a set of queries over real IMDB data. For PostgreSQL, 16% of the estimates for a single join were off by a factor of 10 or more, 32% for two joins and 52% for three, and the errors were mostly underestimates, for the reason you just saw. Underestimates are the dangerous direction. A plan built for 10 rows picks the nested loop with an index lookup per outer row from lesson 9, the best plan for 10 rows and a far more expensive one for 100,000.

The fix is to tell the planner which columns move together. CREATE STATISTICS merchants_geo (dependencies) ON city, country, currency FROM merchants makes ANALYZE measure functional dependencies: for each pair of columns, the fraction of rows in which the value of one decides the value of the other. Here every degree is 1.0. The planner then combines two equality conditions as P(a) x (d + (1 - d) x P(b)), where d is the degree. With d = 1 that is just P(a); with d = 0 it is the old product. The estimate becomes 1,000.

Two more kinds exist: mcv stores the most common combinations of values (it also helps with ranges) and ndistinct counts distinct combinations for GROUP BY. Dependencies only help equality conditions, and they assume the values you ask for belong together: city = 'Amsterdam' AND country = 'JP' is still estimated at 1,000 rows instead of 0. Raising the statistics target doesn't help with any of this, because more detail about each column alone says nothing about pairs.

sections.h: Dynamic programming finds the cheapest join order for the estimates
sections.html:
With estimates for every table and every join, the planner can price any plan. It still has to find the cheapest one, and the number of join orders explodes. A left-deep plan, in which each join adds one table, has n! orders: 6 for 3 tables, 720 for 6, 3.6 million for 10. Bushy plans, which join two joined pairs, add more.

Version 1 lists every order and prices it. That works for 3 tables and is hopeless for 12.

Version 2 notices that orders share parts. Every plan for {merchants, payments, chargebacks} ends with one last join of two smaller sets, and the cheapest plan for a smaller set stays the cheapest whatever is built on top of it. So compute the best plan for every set of tables, smallest sets first: each table alone, then every pair that a join condition connects, then every triple, each built only from best plans already found. That is dynamic programming over sets of tables, the method IBM's System R introduced in 1979 (Selinger and colleagues). It visits 2^n sets instead of n! orders. PostgreSQL searches this way until a query has 12 FROM items (geqo_threshold), then switches to a genetic search that doesn't promise the best plan.

The stepper runs the lab's version on this lesson's query, with all three filters. Its cost counts the rows the joins produce, the intermediate results. Leis and colleagues found that such a simple cost works well: with correct row counts, a cost function that only counted the rows flowing through each operator chose plans about a third faster than PostgreSQL's detailed model in their in-memory tests. With 10 merchants expected, joining merchants to payments first looks cheapest, 1,020 rows against 20,020. With the real 1,000 merchants it does 102,000 rows of work where the other order does 22,000. The search found the cheapest plan for the numbers it was given, and the numbers were wrong.

PostgreSQL makes the same mistake in the Try it, with its own cost model. Expecting 10 merchants, it runs a nested loop with 1,000 bitmap index scans on payments that touch 103,172 buffers, then builds a hash table sized for 1,000 rows that ends up holding 100,000 (EXPLAIN prints Buckets: 131072 (originally 1024)). After CREATE STATISTICS it expects 1,000 merchants and scans payments once into a hash join: 6,542 buffers, 16 times fewer. With every page already in memory, that extra work costs less time than you might expect: on my laptop the first plan took from about as long as the second to 3 times as long. On a table too big for memory, those scattered page visits would become random disk reads.

So the optimizer doesn't always pick the best plan. It picks the best plan for its estimates. When a query is slow, read EXPLAIN ANALYZE from the bottom up and find the first node whose estimated and actual rows differ by 10x or more. Fix that estimate before you add indexes or hints. If a plan must not change at all, PostgreSQL 19 (a release candidate as of November 2026) adds the pg_plan_advice extension to pin planner decisions.

try.title: A wrong estimate picks a nested loop
steps: Drop the dependency statistics (if the last Try it left them) and ANALYZE, so the planner expects 10 merchants again. Run the three-table join under EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Find the lowest node whose estimated rows= and actual rows= differ, and follow the error up the tree.
Recreate the statistics, ANALYZE, and run the same join. Predict which join method replaces the nested loop, and compare the top Buffers lines.
When you are done with this lesson, stop and delete the database: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v.

Expecting 10 merchants, the planner chose a nested loop: one bitmap index scan of payments per merchant, run 1,000 times (loops=1000), feeding a hash table it sized for 1,000 rows and had to grow to hold 100,000. With the right estimate it scans payments once and hash-joins it with the 1,000 merchants. The top Buffers line counts every page the plan touched: 103,172 for the nested loop, which visits the pages of each merchant's 100 payments one bitmap scan at a time, against 6,542 for one pass over payments. Those counts barely change from run to run. The times do: here 207 ms against 211 ms, and across my runs the first plan took from about the same time to 3 times as long, depending on load and on what was cached, so compare plans by their page counts rather than by one timing.

analogy: A satnav picks a route the way a planner picks a plan. It knows the length of every road (the cost model) and predicts the traffic on each (the cardinality estimate), then searches for the fastest combination of roads (the join order). The search is exact, so a bad route almost always comes from a bad traffic guess. And if it assumes two roads have independent traffic when one stadium crowd fills both, it sends you straight into the jam. The analogy breaks once you are moving: a satnav reroutes when the traffic turns out different, while PostgreSQL commits to its plan before the first row and runs it to the end, however wrong the numbers turn out.
world: Payments data is full of correlated columns: country and currency, card scheme and BIN range, merchant and merchant category, and a status that decides which timestamp columns are null. Every search screen that filters on two of them gets an underestimate, and the plan that is fine in a test database with 1,000 rows turns into a nested loop over 100,000 in production. When a settlement report suddenly slows down after a big import, look at EXPLAIN ANALYZE for the first node where estimated and actual rows part ways; often ANALYZE simply hasn't run since the import, and running it is the whole fix. Oracle has the same parts under other names: histograms gathered by DBMS_STATS, column group statistics for correlated columns (its version of CREATE STATISTICS), and adaptive plans that can switch a nested loop to a hash join part way through a query when the rows don't match the estimate. For Hibernate or Panache queries, log the generated SQL and run it under EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) with real parameter values; the estimate for WHERE country = ? AND currency = ? depends on the values you pass.
mistake: The common mistake is treating a slow plan as a bug in the database or a missing index, and forcing a different plan with enable_nestloop = off, a hint or a new index without reading the row counts. People do it because the bad node looks guilty: a nested loop with loops=100000 is easy to blame. Usually the plan was the best one for the estimate it got, and the estimate was wrong, so the next query with the same correlation goes wrong too. The fix is to compare estimated and actual rows node by node in EXPLAIN (ANALYZE), find the lowest node that is off by 10x or more, and fix that estimate: run ANALYZE after bulk loads, raise the statistics target for a badly skewed column, or add CREATE STATISTICS for columns that move together. Pin a plan only when the estimate can't be fixed.

worked.title: Estimate a filter and a join by hand

steps.say: The statistics, as ANALYZE stores them. merchants: 10,000 rows; city has MCV 'Amsterdam' at 0.1; country has MCV 'NL' at 0.1; a dependency city => country of degree 1.0. payments.amount_cents has no MCVs here and a 4-bucket histogram.
Independence first: multiply the two selectivities. This is PostgreSQL's estimate without CREATE STATISTICS.
With the dependency, P(a) x (d + (1 - d) x P(b)): knowing the city fixes the country, so the country condition keeps everything the city condition kept.

A range on the histogram: amount_cents < 1000. 1,000 falls in bucket 2, which runs from 900 to 4,000. Count two whole buckets, add the fraction of bucket 2 below 1,000, divide by the number of buckets.
The join of the 1,000 merchants with payments on p.merchant_id = m.id, both columns with 10,000 distinct values: the two input sizes times 1 / max(distinct, distinct).
steps.code:
rows = 1,000 x 1,000,000 / max(10,000, 10,000) = 100,000
# with the independence estimate of 100 merchants: 10,000, ten times too few

steps.say: The same numbers through the lab's code, which is what the tests check.
steps.code: val city = ColumnStats(rows = 10_000, distinct = 10, mcv = mapOf(0L to 0.1), histogram = null, min = 0, max = 9) val selCity = city.eq(0) // 0.1 val naive = Selectivity.independent(selCity, 0.1) // 0.01 val fixed = Selectivity.withDependency(selCity, 0.1, 1.0) // 0.1 val h = EquiDepthHistogram(longArrayOf(0, 250, 900, 4000, 99000), 4) h.fractionBelow(1000) // 0.508 val joinRows = 1_000.0 * 1_000_000 * joinSelectivity(10_000, 10_000) // 100,000

lab.title: Build a cardinality estimator and a join orderer
steps: Read ColumnStats.analyze() in Statistics.kt: it builds the MCV list and hands the other values to EquiDepthHistogram. Then run the tests once: all 13 fail.
Write the bounds of EquiDepthHistogram and fractionBelow(). The two histogram tests pass.
Write eq() and lt() of ColumnStats, then Selectivity.withDependency(). The estimate tests pass, including the one that shows a 10x underestimate on correlated columns.
In JoinOrder.kt, write joinSelectivity(), JoinGraph.estimate() and bestPlan(). Sets of tables are bitmasks: 0b011 is tables 0 and 1.
Run the tests until all 13 pass. The last one replays the stepper: on the estimates your search picks the plan that does 102,000 rows of work; on the real counts it picks the one that does 22,000.
hints: Bounds: sortedValues[((n - 1).toLong() * i / buckets).toInt()] for i from 0 to buckets. Use Long math, or (n - 1) * i overflows for big columns.
In fractionBelow, handle v <= bounds[0] (0.0) and v > bounds.last() (1.0) first. Then walk i up while bounds[i + 1] < v, and treat a bucket whose two bounds are equal as full.

bestPlan: counting set up from 1 to graph.all visits every subset of a set before the set itself. To walk the non-empty proper subsets of set, start with left = (set - 1) and set and step with left = (left - 1) and set until it is 0; the other side is set xor left.
Skip a split when best[left] or best[right] is null or when graph.connects(left, right) is false. The candidate's cost is best[left].cost + best[right].cost + rows(set); Join computes it for you.

drill.title: Write the join-order search from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write bestPlan(graph, rows): dynamic programming over bitmask sets of tables, with Leaf(t, rows) for one table, Join(left, right, rows) (cost = both sides' costs + its rows), graph.connects(a, b) and graph.all. Skip splits that no join condition connects. Then say how many sets it visits for 10 tables.

answer.html: fun bestPlan(graph: JoinGraph, rows: (Int) -> Double = graph::estimate): Plan { val best = arrayOfNulls<Plan>(graph.all + 1) for (t in 0 until graph.size) best[1 shl t] = Leaf(t, rows(1 shl t)) for (set in 1..graph.all) { // subsets are smaller numbers: done first if (Integer.bitCount(set) < 2) continue val out = rows(set) var left = (set - 1) and set while (left > 0) { val right = set xor left val l = best[left] val r = best[right] if (l != null && r != null && graph.connects(left, right)) { val candidate = Join(l, r, out) if (best[set] == null || candidate.cost < best[set]!!.cost) best[set] = candidate } left = (left - 1) and set } } return best[graph.all] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("join graph not connected") } // 10 tables: 2^10 - 1 = 1,023 non-empty sets, against 3,628,800 left-deep orders.

recap: A cost-based planner lists plans, estimates the rows every step produces, prices each plan with a cost model, and keeps the cheapest. PostgreSQL's units: 1.0 per sequential page, 4.0 per random page, 0.01 per row.
ANALYZE samples 30,000 rows by default and stores per column the null fraction, distinct count, most common values with their frequencies, and a 100-bucket equi-depth histogram, visible in pg_stats.

A range estimate counts whole histogram buckets and assumes an even spread inside one bucket; equality uses the MCV frequency or shares the rest evenly; a join uses rows x rows / max(distinct, distinct).
Conditions on one table are combined by multiplying (independence). Correlated columns make that an underestimate, 10x per extra condition in the Try it, and the error grows with every join above it.
CREATE STATISTICS (dependencies | mcv | ndistinct) teaches the planner which columns move together; dependencies fix equality conditions on correlated columns.

Dynamic programming finds the cheapest join order for the estimates by building the best plan for every set of tables from smaller sets. A bad plan usually means a bad estimate, so compare estimated and actual rows first.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "The optimizer chose a nested loop that took 9 seconds when a hash join takes 3. The optimizer is broken; let's disable nested loops." Explain, using the three parts of an optimizer, what most likely happened and what to do instead.
explain.answer: An optimizer lists possible plans, estimates how many rows each step produces, and prices each plan with a cost model, then keeps the cheapest. The search and the cost formulas are rarely the problem; with the rows it expected, a nested loop probably was the cheapest plan. The likely failure is the estimate. If the outer side was expected to return a few rows and returned tens of thousands, the nested loop ran its inner side once per row. A common cause is conditions on correlated columns, such as city and country, which the planner multiplies as if they were independent, or statistics that are stale after a big load. I'd run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, find the lowest node where estimated and actual rows differ by 10x or more, and fix that: ANALYZE the table, or add CREATE STATISTICS for the columns that move together. Disabling nested loops server-wide would slow every query that looks up a few rows by key.

deeper.html:
Why errors grow with joins. Each join estimate multiplies the estimates of its inputs by a selectivity. If every input is off by a factor of 3, a five-table join can be off by 3^5, about 240. Leis et al. also saw PostgreSQL's estimate for one simple two-join query change with the order of the tables and predicates in the SQL text (3, 9, 128 or 310 rows, against 2,600 real ones), partly because estimates below 1 are rounded up to 1 at different points of the search. Their conclusion: avoid plans that are only good if the estimate is right. A nested loop without an index has a small upside when the estimate holds and a huge downside when it doesn't.

Bigger queries. Above 12 FROM items PostgreSQL's genetic optimizer (GEQO) samples join orders instead of searching all of them. join_collapse_limit and from_collapse_limit (both 8) stop it from reordering long explicit JOIN lists, so above 8 tables the order you write starts to matter.

Adaptive execution and plan stability. Oracle's adaptive plans keep a hash join ready behind a nested loop and switch at run time if the rows from the outer side pass a threshold. PostgreSQL decides everything up front. PostgreSQL 19 adds two extensions for the opposite problem, a plan that flips after an ANALYZE: pg_plan_advice lets you stabilize and control planner decisions, and pg_stash_advice applies that advice automatically by query identifier.

Learned estimators. Research systems train models on samples or on past queries to estimate joins of correlated tables. Leis et al.'s benchmark (JOB) is the standard test for them.
